opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most interesting and underappreciated problems in the field. When people interact with a machine learning system, they're constantly making implicit judgments about how much to rely on it. The trouble is that these systems don't fail the way people expect things to fail.

With a human expert, we have decades of social intuition. If a doctor hesitates or a colleague seems unsure, we pick up on that. We also have a rough sense of where a person's competence lies. Someone great at arithmetic is probably decent at related math. Machine learning models break those intuitions. A model can be superhuman on one task and then fail bizarrely on something that looks trivially easy to us. And it often fails with exactly the same fluency and apparent confidence it shows when it's right.

So you get two failure modes, and they're both real. One is overtrust: people see a system do a few impressive things, generalize, and stop checking its work. That's where automation bias comes in, and it can be dangerous in medicine, hiring, or any high-stakes setting. The other is undertrust: someone sees one strange error, decides the whole thing is junk, and throws away real value. Neither is good. What you want is calibrated trust, where reliance tracks actual reliability, ideally case by case rather than as a blanket attitude.

That's fundamentally a design problem, not just a modeling problem. You can have a well-calibrated model internally, with good probability estimates, and still communicate them so badly that users end up miscalibrated. How do you show uncertainty in a way people actually absorb? How do you help someone build a mental model of where the system is strong and where it's weak? Those are questions about interfaces, visualization, and human cognition as much as about the math.

That's partly why I find interpretability so exciting in this context. If we can understand what's going on inside these models, even partially, we may be able to give users signals that reflect what the system is doing, rather than just a surface impression. But we're still early, and I think there's a lot of room for creative work on how people and these systems can understand each other better.

r001.rationale: It explicitly calls for calibrated trust, where reliance tracks the system’s actual reliability case by case, rather than a blanket increase in trust.

r002.rationale: It says users may discard real value after seeing an error, communicating that the system can still be useful despite sometimes being wrong.

r003.rationale: It mentions users stopping their checks, but does not identify teaching users how to test outputs as a design challenge.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the thing people miss is that trust isn't a dial you want to turn all the way up. The goal isn't maximum trust, it's accurate trust. You want people to trust the system exactly as much as it deserves in a given situation, and no more and no less.

And that turns out to be really hard, because these systems fail in ways that don't match human intuition. If I work with a human colleague, I build up a pretty good model over time of where they're strong and where they're shaky, and I know when to double-check them. With a machine learning model, the failure modes are strange. It might be brilliant on something that looks hard and then fall apart on something that looks trivially easy. So people's instincts about when to be skeptical are just miscalibrated from the start.

What you end up seeing is two failure modes. One is over-trust, where the system has been right a hundred times in a row and people stop looking, and then the one time it's confidently wrong it goes straight through. The other is under-trust, where someone gets burned once and just stops using the thing entirely, even though on average it would have helped them a lot. Both of those are bad outcomes, and interestingly, both of them are design problems rather than purely modeling problems.

So I think of this as a visualization and interface question as much as anything. Can you show someone not just the answer but some sense of the system's uncertainty, or the regions where it's been reliable before? Can you make its reasoning, or at least its evidence, inspectable? Those are things that help a person build a mental model of the tool. And that's really what calibration is, it's helping the user build an accurate mental model so their trust tracks reality. Without that, you're asking people to make high-stakes decisions based on a black box, and they'll either defer to it blindly or ignore it, and neither is what you want.

r001.rationale: It says the goal is accurate trust: users should trust the system as much as it deserves in each situation, neither more nor less.

r002.rationale: It says users may stop using the system after an error even though it would have helped on average, conveying that it can remain useful despite occasional mistakes.

r003.rationale: The response discusses double-checking, uncertainty, and making evidence inspectable, but does not identify teaching users how to test the system’s outputs as a design challenge.

astra-6.text:
Well, you don’t want people to trust a system too much, but you also don’t want them to dismiss something that could be useful. The goal is to help them understand when to rely on it and when to question it.

Machine learning makes that difficult because a system can be remarkably good in one situation and fail in another that looks very similar to a person. And the interface can give you a misleading impression. A polished presentation or a convincing explanation can make an answer feel reliable without actually making it more reliable.

So the design challenge is to make the system’s capabilities and limitations understandable in the context of what someone is doing. Can they see where it tends to make mistakes? Can they recognize when they’re outside the situations where it works well? That’s a more demanding goal than simply making the system seem trustworthy.

r001.rationale: It says users should know when to rely on the system and when to question it, and explains that polished presentation can make answers seem more reliable than they are.

r002.rationale: It describes the system as useful in some situations while still capable of failing in similar-looking situations.

r003.rationale: It says users should recognize where the system makes mistakes and when it may fail, but does not identify teaching them how to test its outputs as a design challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
Because you don’t want people to trust a system too much, and you don’t want them to trust it too little. You want their trust to match what the system can actually do. And that’s surprisingly hard with machine learning, because a system can be very good in one situation and fail in another that looks almost identical to a person.

The way you present it matters enormously. A polished interface or a confident-sounding answer can make something seem more reliable than it is. And an explanation can be persuasive without actually helping you judge whether the answer is correct.

So the design question is: How do you help someone develop a useful understanding of where this thing works, where it doesn’t, and when they should check its output? That’s a much more subtle goal than simply making the system understandable or getting people to trust it.

r001.rationale: The response says users’ trust should match what the system can actually do, rather than simply be increased.

r002.rationale: It describes the system working well in some situations and failing in others, while asking users to understand where it works and where it does not.

r003.rationale: It discusses helping users know when to check outputs, but does not identify teaching them how to test those outputs as a design challenge.
